Module: Module 00 · Start Here: Your Organisation Journey
Learning objective: See how the course is organised and decide which module you most need and when to reach it.
Why this source: 0 resources. This is an orientation lesson about how the course itself works, so no outside reading would add anything the course map does not already give. Sending learners to reading before they start would only delay the first exercise.

Module: Module 00 · Start Here: Your Organisation Journey
Learning objective: Describe your organisation's form, stage and open questions so you can choose the examples that fit you.
Recommended source: The Global State of Social Enterprise
Organisation: British Council, with Social Enterprise UK
Why this source: Shows how purpose-led organisations are actually structured across 27 countries, from charities and cooperatives to companies, and why there is no single definition. Helps you find vocabulary that fits your own context.
What to look for: Read the sections on definitions and legal forms, then the findings for the countries closest to where you work.
Use in lesson: Use it when completing your profile, to find the form and terms nearest your own and see what others in your country chose.

Module: Module 00 · Start Here: Your Organisation Journey
Learning objective: Describe your organisation's form, stage and open questions so you can choose the examples that fit you.
Recommended source: Social Enterprise: A Typology of the Field Contextualized in Latin America
Why this source: Places organisations on a spectrum from purely nonprofit to purely commercial, with hybrids between. Useful for describing a mixed structure honestly. It is old (2003), so use it for the concept, not current law.
What to look for: The typology of hybrid models and the spectrum from nonprofit to for-profit, with the Latin American case examples.
Use in lesson: Use it if you are a hybrid or unsure where you sit, to describe your structure and note the open questions in your profile.

Module: Module 00 · Start Here: Your Organisation Journey
Learning objective: Rate how developed each part of your organisation is today, with evidence, and name your three priorities.
Recommended source: Pact's Organizational Performance Index: Domains and Sub-domains
Why this source: A practitioner-tested list of organisational capability domains and sub-domains, updated in 2023 to add resilience. Gives you ready-made areas to rate instead of inventing your own.
What to look for: Skim the domains and sub-domains, then choose the eight to twelve areas that matter at your stage and size.
Use in lesson: Use it to choose the capability areas in your health check and to word the evidence you would expect for each rating.

Module: Module 00 · Start Here: Your Organisation Journey
Learning objective: Rate how developed each part of your organisation is today, with evidence, and name your three priorities.
Recommended source: OCAT Guidelines and Toolkit (Organizational Capacity Analysis Tool)
Why this source: A self-reflection process for grassroots organisations: staff reflect first, then score together with documents to hand. Shows how to make self-assessment collaborative rather than box-ticking. Designed for a funder's partners, so adapt it.
What to look for: Read the guidelines on the pre-visit reflection and group scoring, then adapt the toolkit templates to your own capability areas.
Use in lesson: Use it for the 'involve someone else' step: compare differing ratings and attach documents as evidence to each score.

Learning objective: Write down the unmet need first, then a purpose statement that stays meaningful if your activities change.
Why this source: Field-tested guidance on listening to communities, including marginalised people, before designing anything. Helps you record what you actually heard instead of confirming your own idea. Dated 2013 but the methods remain standard.
What to look for: The planning phase (objectives, questions, who to include) and the annexes with sample tools such as focus-group guides.
Use in lesson: Use it for the exercise's evidence gap: plan a realistic way to talk with affected people, including those who may disagree with your idea.

Learning objective: Write down the unmet need first, then a purpose statement that stays meaningful if your activities change.
Why this source: Offers a counterweight to a needs-only view by starting from what people and communities already have. Helps you avoid a purpose that treats people only as problems to be fixed.
What to look for: The asset mapping tools, especially the capacity inventories, and the talking-point materials explaining the approach.
Use in lesson: Use it when you describe the need: record community strengths and existing local solutions alongside the gap you found.

Learning objective: Scan the outside environment and map who else is active, so your strategy responds to real conditions.
Why this source: Rates freedom of association, assembly and expression in 195+ countries and tracks trends. A quick, comparable read on the political and legal context for civil society work, especially where civic space is restricted.
What to look for: Look up your country profile, its rating and recent trend notes, and what restrictions affect organisations like yours.
Use in lesson: Use it for the political and legal parts of your context scan, and to note constraints or risks to carry forward.

Learning objective: Scan the outside environment and map who else is active, so your strategy responds to real conditions.
Recommended source: SWOT Analysis: Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats (Chapter 3, Section 14)
Organisation: Community Tool Box, University of Kansas
Why this source: A plain, step-by-step SWOT written for community groups, with advice on involving diverse people and not underselling strengths. Treats SWOT as a team conversation, not a form.
What to look for: How to run the group brainstorm, and the TOWS matrix at the end for turning observations into strategic options.
Use in lesson: Use it for the exercise's context scan: write each point with a source, then note what it means for your strategy.

Learning objective: Scan the outside environment and map who else is active, so your strategy responds to real conditions.
Recommended source: Strategic Planning in Times of Uncertainty: A Practical Framework for Nonprofit Leaders
Why this source: A recent five-step framework for planning when conditions shift. Helps you decide when a new law, funding change or crisis should reopen your strategy rather than being absorbed quietly.
What to look for: Step 1 (scope the critical decisions), the stakeholder engagement step, and the advice to narrow to three to five priorities.
Use in lesson: Use it when setting your yearly review: write down which kinds of change would make you redo this scan.

Learning objective: Identify who benefits, pays, decides and influences, and plan how to engage each priority group.
Earlier sources (action): IDEO Design Kit: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design [KEEP]
Why this source: A short tool for listing stakeholders, sorting them by interest and power, and choosing how to engage each. Written for policy influencing but works for any organisation. From 2009, though not superseded.
What to look for: The steps for identifying and categorising stakeholders, and the influence-map example that turns the grid into an engagement strategy.
Use in lesson: Use it to build your stakeholder map and decide how to engage each priority group, including those with high interest but little power.

Learning objective: Identify who benefits, pays, decides and influences, and plan how to engage each priority group.
Earlier sources (action): IDEO Design Kit: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design [KEEP]
Recommended source: IDEO Design Kit: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design
Why this source: Fifty-seven field methods for interviewing, synthesising and prototyping with communities. Helps you understand the beneficiary, payer, decider and influencer roles by talking to real people rather than guessing.
What to look for: The Hear (inspiration) methods on interviews and immersion, especially stakeholder mapping and community-driven discovery.
Use in lesson: Use it when you test your map: interview people in each role and note where your assumptions about benefit, payment and influence were wrong.

Learning objective: Identify who benefits, pays, decides and influences, and plan how to engage each priority group.
Earlier sources (action): IDEO Design Kit: The Field Guide to Human-Centered Design [KEEP]
Recommended source: Powercube: Understanding Power for Social Change
Organisation: Institute of Development Studies, University of Sussex
Why this source: Gives language and tools for seeing visible, hidden and invisible power, so you do not overlook people with high interest but little power. Adds a depth the influence-interest grid cannot.
What to look for: The Power Analysis section on forms, spaces and levels of power, and the Power Matrix in the Strategic Action section.
Use in lesson: Use it after drawing your grid to ask whose voice is missing and who may be blocked from taking part.

Learning objective: Describe the future condition you want to help create, in plain words people can picture and test.
Earlier sources (action): Strategic Planning in Times of Uncertainty [MOVE]; Three Horizons Framework [UPDATE]
Why this source: Separates the future you want (vision) from the work you do (mission) and gives a three-step process: gather input, distil, test drafts with different audiences. Free and openly licensed (CC BY 4.0).
What to look for: The distinction between vision and mission, and the three-step drafting process, especially testing with different audiences.
Use in lesson: Use it for the exercise's last step: test your one-sentence vision with someone affected and see what they picture.

Learning objective: Describe the future condition you want to help create, in plain words people can picture and test.
Earlier sources (action): Strategic Planning in Times of Uncertainty [MOVE]; Three Horizons Framework [UPDATE]
Organisation: New Philanthropy Capital (NPC), crediting International Futures Forum
Why this source: A simple way to discuss the move from today's system to the future you want, and your role among many others. Includes a Scottish elder-care case study and a group exercise.
What to look for: The three horizons diagram, the SHINE case study and the 'Three Voices' group exercise.
Use in lesson: Use it in a team session to place your vision beyond your own services: what is ending, what is emerging, what future you want.

Learning objective: Describe the future condition you want to help create, in plain words people can picture and test.
Earlier sources (action): Strategic Planning in Times of Uncertainty [MOVE]; Three Horizons Framework [UPDATE]
Why this source: Gives internationally agreed conditions (169 targets) that many organisations contribute to. Helps you check your vision describes a condition in the world, not a service list.
What to look for: Browse the goals and targets nearest your issue, and use the annual progress reports to see current trends.
Use in lesson: Use it to see which global condition your vision contributes to, then write your own sentence in everyday language rather than copying target wording.

Learning objective: Draft a one-sentence mission that names who you serve, what changes and your approach, and use it as a decision filter.
Earlier sources (action): Strategic Planning for Nonprofits and NGOs [MOVE]
Recommended source: Proclaiming Your Dream: Developing Vision and Mission Statements (Chapter 8, Section 2)
Organisation: Community Tool Box, University of Kansas
Why this source: Plain explanation of what a mission statement is and is not, with a step-by-step drafting process that involves community members. Complements the lesson's sentence formula.
What to look for: The mission statement characteristics and examples, then the steps from gathering input to community agreement and sharing.
Use in lesson: Use it to test your drafted sentence against the characteristics and plan who should read it before you finalise.

Learning objective: Draft a one-sentence mission that names who you serve, what changes and your approach, and use it as a decision filter.
Earlier sources (action): Strategic Planning for Nonprofits and NGOs [MOVE]
Recommended source: What Are Intended Impact and Theory of Change and How Can Nonprofits Use Them?
Why this source: Defines intended impact as who you serve, where and what changes, with an example of narrowing focus. Helps you fill the people, geography and change parts of your mission sentence.
What to look for: The who, where and what definition of intended impact, and the YW Boston example of sharpening focus.
Use in lesson: Use it if your draft tries to serve everyone: tighten the people and place, then check the sentence still names an approach.

Learning objective: Draft a one-sentence mission that names who you serve, what changes and your approach, and use it as a decision filter.
Earlier sources (action): Strategic Planning for Nonprofits and NGOs [MOVE]
Recommended source: The governance of social enterprises: Mission drift and accountability challenges in hybrid organizations
Organisation: Alnoor Ebrahim, Julie Battilana and Johanna Mair (Research in Organizational Behavior)
Why this source: Research on how organisations that trade for a social purpose can drift from their mission, and how boards can keep both goals in view. Backs up using the mission as a decision filter.
What to look for: The difference between differentiated and integrated models, and the sections on accountability for dual performance and to multiple stakeholders.
Use in lesson: Use it if you trade or take contracts: set the mission tests you will apply before accepting income that pulls you off course.
Access: Journal article (publisher or library access; check author repositories)

Learning objective: Turn a few core values into observable behaviours, boundaries and evidence, and test them against a hard decision.
Why this source: Four principles (Beneficiaries First, Integrity, Openness, Right to Be Safe) with guidance for boards, staff and volunteers. Shows ethics as questions to ask, not slogans. Developed for UK charities but useful anywhere.
What to look for: The guidance for governing bodies, staff and volunteers, and the section on resolving conflicts between principles.
Use in lesson: Use it when writing each value's behaviour and boundary, and when choosing the difficult decision you test your values against.

Learning objective: Turn a few core values into observable behaviours, boundaries and evidence, and test them against a hard decision.
Why this source: A classic argument that most values statements are hollow, with a way to separate core, aspirational, permission-to-play and accidental values. Helps you choose the few you can really practise.
What to look for: The four types of value, and the advice to build values into hiring, performance review and dismissal.
Use in lesson: Use it when cutting your list to three to five: ask which you already live, which you aspire to and which are simply expected.

Learning objective: Compare the forms you are considering against control, surplus, funding and reporting, and state your current preference.
Recommended source: A Guide to Legal Forms for Social Enterprises in South Africa
Organisation: Bertha Centre for Social Innovation and Entrepreneurship, UCT Graduate School of Business
Why this source: Compares nonprofit, for-profit and hybrid forms on governance, surplus, funding and reporting, the same four questions as this lesson. A clear model for your own comparison. South African law and 2016, so check local rules.
What to look for: The overview of legal forms, the business model mapping step and the selection guidance at the end.
Use in lesson: Use it as a pattern for your comparison table, replacing the South African detail with advice from your own country.

Learning objective: Compare the forms you are considering against control, surplus, funding and reporting, and state your current preference.
Organisation: Thomson Reuters Foundation (TrustLaw), hosted by ANDE
Why this source: A free country-by-country guide covering registration, licences, governance duties and tax in eight ASEAN countries. Shows how differently the same choice plays out across jurisdictions. Dated 2018.
What to look for: Pick your country chapter for the registration options and governance obligations, then compare with one other country.
Use in lesson: Use it after your comparison to draft questions for a local lawyer or registrar. It does not replace local advice.

Learning objective: Compare the forms you are considering against control, surplus, funding and reporting, and state your current preference.
Organisation: Lilly Family School of Philanthropy, Indiana University
Why this source: Country reports on how easy it is to run a philanthropic organisation, covering legal forms, tax incentives and the political and economic setting in 95 countries. Useful for checking what your own country allows.
What to look for: Find your country's report and read the parts on legal forms and ease of operating, then compare with your shortlisted forms.
Use in lesson: Use it to check which forms your country's law recognises and what tax treatment follows, before you ask an adviser.

Learning objective: State where you add unique value, and the choices that follow, including what you will not do.
Recommended source: How Nonprofits Can Map Their Programs to Their Strategy
Why this source: A simple matrix placing each programme by how well it fits your impact goals and how it is funded, then deciding to grow, improve, maintain or exit. Makes 'saying no' concrete.
What to look for: The programme strategy map matrix, and the downloadable guide and Excel template linked from the article.
Use in lesson: Use it to list the choices your positioning statement implies: which activities fit, which to refer on, and which to stop.

Learning objective: State where you add unique value, and the choices that follow, including what you will not do.
Organisation: Michael E. Porter, Harvard Business Review
Why this source: The original argument that strategy means a unique position and deliberate trade-offs, including what not to do. Written for companies, but the logic fits any organisation choosing where to focus.
What to look for: The sections on strategic position and trade-offs, and the warning about trying to serve every customer.
Use in lesson: Use it to test your comparative advantage: is it a distinct position you can sustain, or good intentions anyone could claim?

Learning objective: Set a few external and internal strategic objectives with codes, a picture of success and an owner, within your real capacity.
Recommended source: How Nonprofits and NGOs Can Get Real Value from Strategic Planning
Why this source: Explains how to turn impact goals into a few multiyear priorities, estimate the resources needed and avoid unfocused plans. Directly backs keeping the set small and checking feasibility.
What to look for: The 'Set Strategic Priorities' and 'Estimate Resources' sections, and the five ways planning goes wrong.
Use in lesson: Use it for the feasibility step: test each objective against time, money and skills, and record what you will postpone.

Learning objective: Set a few external and internal strategic objectives with codes, a picture of success and an owner, within your real capacity.
Why this source: Explains that an objective states direction and key results make progress visible, with a public-service worked example. A useful preview of how your objectives will later become measurable.
What to look for: The four qualities of a strong objective, and the Healthcare.gov example of one objective with measurable key results.
Use in lesson: Use it to phrase each 'picture of success' clearly and concretely. Leave key results and numbers for Modules 6 and 13.

Learning objective: Explain, in a reasoned and testable way, how and why your work could contribute to change, and separate what you control, influence and only contribute to.
Earlier sources (action): Describe the Theory of Change — BetterEvaluation [KEEP]
Recommended source: Describe the theory of change (Manager's guide to evaluation)
Why this source: Explains in plain practitioner language what a theory of change must include: causal pathway, context, other actors, assumptions and unintended results.
What to look for: Read the options for developing and representing a theory of change, and note how it treats other influences on the result.
Use in lesson: Use it before you write your first if… then… because… statement.

Learning objective: Explain, in a reasoned and testable way, how and why your work could contribute to change, and separate what you control, influence and only contribute to.
Earlier sources (action): Describe the Theory of Change — BetterEvaluation [KEEP]
Recommended source: Theory of Change in Ten Steps
Why this source: A short, worked handbook written for charities. It takes you from situation analysis to assumptions with one running example, which makes the sequence easy to copy.
What to look for: Steps 3 to 7 (impact, outcomes, activities, change mechanisms, sequencing) and step 10 on assumptions. The 'One Small Step' example shows a finished pathway.
Use in lesson: Use it while building one pathway for your first external objective.

Learning objective: Describe the problem, its causes and who experiences it, with the people affected, and choose a scope you can realistically influence.
Earlier sources (action): Start by Learning About Users and Their Needs — GOV.UK Service Manual [KEEP]; Problem Tree Analysis — Overseas Development Institute [KEEP]
Why this source: A two-page, plain explanation of the trunk, roots and branches method, with a worked example showing how a focus group changed a project design.
What to look for: The step-by-step description and the Kenya HIV/AIDS example. Note the advice to use a small group of six to eight people.
Use in lesson: Use it in your problem-tree workshop with people affected by the issue.

Learning objective: Describe the problem, its causes and who experiences it, with the people affected, and choose a scope you can realistically influence.
Earlier sources (action): Start by Learning About Users and Their Needs — GOV.UK Service Manual [KEEP]; Problem Tree Analysis — Overseas Development Institute [KEEP]
Recommended source: Defining and Analyzing the Problem (Community Tool Box, Chapter 17, Section 3)
Organisation: Center for Community Health and Development, University of Kansas
Why this source: Adds the discipline of defining a problem as a need, not a solution, and shows the 'but why' and force-field methods for testing causes.
What to look for: The four steps: clarify, define, decide, analyse. Read 'defining the problem in terms of needs, not solutions' closely.
Use in lesson: Use it to check your problem statement does not hide a favoured solution.

Learning objective: Describe the problem, its causes and who experiences it, with the people affected, and choose a scope you can realistically influence.
Earlier sources (action): Start by Learning About Users and Their Needs — GOV.UK Service Manual [KEEP]; Problem Tree Analysis — Overseas Development Institute [KEEP]
Recommended source: Start by learning about users and their needs
Why this source: Shows how to replace assumptions with evidence about people, tasks and barriers, and how to write needs without prescribing a solution.
What to look for: The sections on researching users, writing user needs and validating them against research evidence.
Use in lesson: Use it before finalising your problem statement, especially if you are a startup or social enterprise with a product in mind.

Learning objective: Draft an impact statement that names whose lives or conditions should change, and state honestly that the claim is contribution, not sole attribution.
Why this source: A clear overview of how to build and test a credible contribution story when many actors and conditions affect the result.
What to look for: The six steps, especially developing the theory of change and assembling then challenging the contribution story.
Use in lesson: Use it when your impact depends on other actors, to decide what you can honestly claim.

Learning objective: Draft an impact statement that names whose lives or conditions should change, and state honestly that the claim is contribution, not sole attribution.
Recommended source: Contribution Analysis: An Approach to Exploring Cause and Effect (ILAC Brief 16)
Organisation: John Mayne, Institutional Learning and Change (CGIAR)
Why this source: The original four-page statement of the method by its main author. It explains why attribution is the wrong ask for most programmes.
What to look for: Section 2 (the six steps) and Section 3, the three levels of contribution analysis from minimalist to indirect influence.
Use in lesson: Use it to word the limits of what you could establish in your impact statement.

Learning objective: Sequence short, medium and long-term outcomes backwards from your impact, with the kind of evidence that would show each one is happening, including unequal effects.
Why this source: Focuses on changes in behaviour, relationships and actions of the people you work with, which is where most outcomes actually sit.
What to look for: The three spheres (control, influence, concern) and the four stages. Skip the evaluation-planning detail at first.
Use in lesson: Use it when your outcomes are about behaviour or relationships rather than service totals.

Learning objective: Sequence short, medium and long-term outcomes backwards from your impact, with the kind of evidence that would show each one is happening, including unequal effects.
Recommended source: Outcome Mapping: Building Learning and Reflection into Development Programs
Why this source: The original handbook, with workshop worksheets. Its 'progress markers' turn an outcome into a ladder of observable changes, without yet becoming indicators.
What to look for: Chapter 3, Step 4 (outcome challenge) and Step 5 (graduated progress markers).
Use in lesson: Use it to describe the kind of evidence for each outcome before Module 6 turns it into indicators.

Learning objective: Sequence short, medium and long-term outcomes backwards from your impact, with the kind of evidence that would show each one is happening, including unequal effects.
Recommended source: Outcome Mapping + Equity, Gender, and Social Justice (OM+)
Organisation: Heidi Schaeffer and Sonal Zaveri, Outcome Mapping Learning Community
Why this source: Adds power, inclusion and equity questions to outcome thinking, so you look for unequal and unintended effects, not only the hoped-for result.
What to look for: The principles for equity-focused outcomes and who defines progress. Available in French, Spanish and Hindi.
Use in lesson: Use it when checking whether any outcome could benefit some groups and leave others behind.

Learning objective: List the products and services your activities deliver, with quality and reach as well as quantity, and keep them separate from outcomes.
Recommended source: Glossary of Key Terms in Evaluation and Results-Based Management for Sustainable Development (2nd edition)
Why this source: The international reference for what counts as an input, output, outcome and impact, so your definitions match what funders and evaluators expect.
What to look for: Look up 'output', 'outcome' and 'results chain' and compare them with the lesson's wording.
Use in lesson: Use it when checking that nothing on your outputs list is really an outcome.

Learning objective: List the actions needed to deliver each output, tested for feasibility and acceptability in the local context.
Earlier sources (action): Programme Design and Performance Management Toolkit — FCDO [UPDATE]
Recommended source: FCDO Programme Operating Framework (formerly Smart Rules)
Why this source: Shows how a major donor expects programmes to be designed, delivered and risk-managed, which helps you check your activities will stand up to funder scrutiny.
What to look for: The programme delivery and risk sections. The rules apply to FCDO-funded work, so treat them as a model unless you hold FCDO funding.
Use in lesson: Use it when turning outputs into a realistic sequence of activities.
Region: UK (donor rules; useful as a model)

Learning objective: List the actions needed to deliver each output, tested for feasibility and acceptability in the local context.
Earlier sources (action): Programme Design and Performance Management Toolkit — FCDO [UPDATE]
Recommended source: Adaptive management: what it means for CSOs
Why this source: Explains how to plan activities you expect to adjust, which suits the lesson's point that a sound plan can fail if local conditions are ignored.
What to look for: The sections on when adaptive approaches suit a programme and the organisational changes they need.
Use in lesson: Use it when testing whether each activity is feasible and acceptable locally, and what you will change if it is not.

Learning objective: List the people, money, skills, relationships and access you need, what you already have, and the gaps.
Why this source: 0 resources. This is a short listing exercise and costing is taught properly in Module 9, where the sources belong. No verified free source added real value beyond the lesson.

Learning objective: Make the critical assumptions in your pathway specific and testable, rank them by uncertainty and importance, and decide what evidence would change your plan.
Earlier sources (action): Theory of Change in Practice — USAID Learning Lab [REPLACE]
Recommended source: Review of the use of 'Theory of Change' in international development
Why this source: Shows why making assumptions explicit is the heart of theory of change thinking, and how to treat them as propositions to check with stakeholders.
What to look for: Section 4 'Why are assumptions so important?' and Section 7 on evidence use.
Use in lesson: Use it to turn hidden assumptions into questions you can investigate.

Learning objective: Make the critical assumptions in your pathway specific and testable, rank them by uncertainty and importance, and decide what evidence would change your plan.
Earlier sources (action): Theory of Change in Practice — USAID Learning Lab [REPLACE]
Why this source: A checklist to judge how strong the evidence behind each assumption is: voice and inclusion, appropriateness, triangulation, contribution and transparency.
What to look for: Use the checklist to rate the evidence for each critical assumption. The principles are in the downloadable spreadsheet.
Use in lesson: Use it to record current evidence and decide what to test next.

Lesson: 2.9 Test, write and use your Theory of Change
Learning objective: Write a one-page narrative per pathway, test it with people who know the issue, and set a version and review plan so it drives real decisions.
Earlier sources (action): Theory of Change Methodological Brief — UNICEF and BetterEvaluation [KEEP]
Recommended source: Theory of Change Thinking in Practice: A Stepwise Approach
Organisation: Marjan van Es, Irene Guijt and Isabel Vogel, Hivos
Why this source: Written for partner organisations in many countries, it treats theory of change as a living tool for learning and adapting, not a one-off diagram.
What to look for: Quality of ToC practice (pp. 28 to 32), then Step 7 (learning priorities) and Step 8 (using and adapting the ToC).
Use in lesson: Use it to plan how you will test the theory with others and set your version and review rhythm.
Region: Global (Hivos works with partners in the Global South)

Lesson: 2.9 Test, write and use your Theory of Change
Learning objective: Write a one-page narrative per pathway, test it with people who know the issue, and set a version and review plan so it drives real decisions.
Earlier sources (action): Theory of Change Methodological Brief — UNICEF and BetterEvaluation [KEEP]
Recommended source: Theory of Change (Methodological Brief: Impact Evaluation No. 2)
Organisation: Patricia Rogers, UNICEF Office of Research and BetterEvaluation
Why this source: A detailed, authoritative method for developing a results chain and testing it against assumptions, indicators and evidence.
What to look for: Section 3 (how to develop a theory of change), Section 7 (presentation) and Section 9 (common challenges).
Use in lesson: Use it when facilitating a full theory of change workshop or preparing an evaluation.

Learning objective: List the capabilities and functions your strategy needs, and decide for each whether you do it in-house, share it with partners or contract it out.
Earlier sources (action): Operating Models: How Nonprofits Get from Strategy to Results — Bridgespan [KEEP]
Recommended source: Operating Models: How Nonprofits Get from Strategy to Results
Why this source: Shows how to start from strategy and the critical capabilities, not an org chart, with three case studies and eight design practices.
What to look for: The four operating model elements (structure and accountability, priorities and resources, leadership and culture, critical capabilities) and the 'start with strategic clarity' practice.
Use in lesson: Use it before drawing your structure, to list capabilities and note which you will build, share or contract out.
Region: Global (US-based, case studies from several countries)

Learning objective: Map your roles and reporting lines in a simple organisation chart that fits your stage and legal form.
Why this source: 0 resources in this pass. The search limit was reached before a strong, free source on small-organisation structure (functional, matrix, network or hub) could be verified. Several guides found were paywalled or generic. Recommend a follow-up search, ideally for a network or hub structure source with Global South examples.

Learning objective: Describe the governance structure your legal form requires and the one you want to build, with clear lines between governing body, management and advisers.
Earlier sources (action): Charity Governance Code — Charity Governance Code Steering Group [UPDATE]
Organisation: Charity Governance Code Steering Group (ACEVO, NCVO, WCVA, Chartered Governance Institute and others)
Why this source: Eight principles and 41 outcomes for good governance, including a practical 'apply or explain' approach that suits member-based, corporate-trustee and other forms. UK voluntary code, not law.
What to look for: The principles on leadership and decision making, and the behaviours and evidence markers listed under each principle.
Use in lesson: Use it to define how governance and management differ in your organisation.

Learning objective: Describe the governance structure your legal form requires and the one you want to build, with clear lines between governing body, management and advisers.
Earlier sources (action): Charity Governance Code — Charity Governance Code Steering Group [UPDATE]
Why this source: The original international statement of what a cooperative is and how members control it. Useful if members, not owners or trustees, are your top decision body.
What to look for: Principle 2 (democratic member control) and Principle 3 (member economic participation).
Use in lesson: Use it if your legal form is a cooperative, to describe who holds which decisions.

Learning objective: Describe the governance structure your legal form requires and the one you want to build, with clear lines between governing body, management and advisers.
Earlier sources (action): Charity Governance Code — Charity Governance Code Steering Group [UPDATE]
Why this source: The international benchmark on how shareholders and boards share rights and duties in companies. Written for listed firms, but the division of roles applies to any company.
What to look for: The chapters on shareholder rights and on the responsibilities of the board. Skim stock-market sections.
Use in lesson: Use it if you are a company or social enterprise, to separate board decisions from shareholder decisions.

Learning objective: List the decisions only your governing body can take and build a simple governance calendar, including how a founder who is also a director is managed.
Earlier sources (action): Decision-making for Charity Trustees (CC27) — Charity Commission for England and Wales [KEEP]
Organisation: Charity Commission for England and Wales
Why this source: England and Wales regulator guidance on lawful, informed decisions, joint responsibility, delegation and recording decisions. Other countries have different law, but the principles are widely used.
What to look for: The seven decision-making principles, 'Clearly record your decisions' and 'Delegating decision-making'.
Use in lesson: Use it to define reserved matters and what the minutes should record.

Learning objective: List the decisions only your governing body can take and build a simple governance calendar, including how a founder who is also a director is managed.
Earlier sources (action): Decision-making for Charity Trustees (CC27) — Charity Commission for England and Wales [KEEP]

Organisation: World Bank (Jody Zall Kusek and Ray C. Rist)
Why this source: A classic open-access handbook that shows how to track performance against targets and use the results to manage. Older (2004), but the monitoring logic is still standard.
What to look for: Step 6, monitoring for results, plus Steps 4 and 5 on baselines and targets, to link back to lessons 6.3 and 6.4.
Use in lesson: Use it when you design the planned-versus-actual routine and decide who reviews performance data and when.

Module: Module 06 · MEAL: Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability & Learning
Learning objective: Design a simple dashboard and review routine that compares planned with actual results, explains gaps before reacting and shares data with those who can act.
Why this source: Tested rules for choosing simple charts, labelling clearly and making them accessible. UK government guidance, but the design rules apply anywhere. Keeps dashboards readable by frontline staff and participants.
What to look for: The sections on choosing chart types, colour contrast and text alternatives. Use them to keep the dashboard to a few clear charts.
Use in lesson: Use it when you design your dashboard and write the short commentary beside the traffic-light status.

Module: Module 06 · MEAL: Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability & Learning
Learning objective: Draft an evaluation plan: choose purpose and type, the criteria and questions, who evaluates, and how findings will be used and published.
Earlier sources (action): Applying Evaluation Criteria Thoughtfully [KEEP]; The Magenta Book [REMOVE]
Why this source: The official explanation of relevance, coherence, effectiveness, efficiency, impact and sustainability, including unintended and unequal effects.
What to look for: The introduction and the chapter on each criterion, including how to apply the criteria thoughtfully rather than as a fixed checklist.
Use in lesson: Use it to choose criteria and write evaluation questions, and to challenge whether objectives are relevant and sustainable.

Module: Module 06 · MEAL: Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability & Learning
Learning objective: Draft an evaluation plan: choose purpose and type, the criteria and questions, who evaluates, and how findings will be used and published.
Earlier sources (action): Applying Evaluation Criteria Thoughtfully [KEEP]; The Magenta Book [REMOVE]
Recommended source: CDC Program Evaluation Framework Action Guide
Organisation: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
Why this source: A step-by-step how-to with fillable worksheets for scoping, questions, evidence and using findings, with equity and community engagement built in. US public health origin, but widely transferable.
What to look for: The six steps, especially Focus Evaluation Questions and Design, and the appendix worksheets on evaluability, interest holders and data collection strategy.
Use in lesson: Use it to choose the evaluation type, draft questions and methods, and plan how findings will be used.

Module: Module 06 · MEAL: Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability & Learning
Learning objective: Draft an evaluation plan: choose purpose and type, the criteria and questions, who evaluates, and how findings will be used and published.
Earlier sources (action): Applying Evaluation Criteria Thoughtfully [KEEP]; The Magenta Book [REMOVE]
Why this source: Locally developed principles that put participants and context first, and challenge evaluation designs imported from outside. Useful for deciding who evaluates and how findings are shared.
What to look for: The five principles (Powerful, Technical, Ethical, Africa-centric, Connected) and the commitments on reciprocity and 'nothing about us without us'.
Use in lesson: Use it when you decide whether to evaluate internally or commission someone, and how participants judge results and receive findings.

Module: Module 06 · MEAL: Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability & Learning
Learning objective: Design a feedback and complaints mechanism with several channels, a route outside the delivery team, response times and a way to close the loop.
Earlier sources (action): Core Humanitarian Standard on Quality and Accountability [UPDATE]
Recommended source: Core Humanitarian Standard on Quality and Accountability (2024)
Organisation: CHS Alliance, Groupe URD and Sphere
Why this source: Nine commitments built around communities, with specific commitments on communication, participation and feedback, and on complaints. A recognised benchmark that applies beyond humanitarian work.
What to look for: Commitments 4 and 5 and their key actions and organisational responsibilities, in the booklet or the free interactive handbook.
Use in lesson: Use it to check your feedback channels, response times and sensitive-concerns route against a recognised standard.

Module: Module 06 · MEAL: Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability & Learning
Learning objective: Design a feedback and complaints mechanism with several channels, a route outside the delivery team, response times and a way to close the loop.
Earlier sources (action): Core Humanitarian Standard on Quality and Accountability [UPDATE]
Recommended source: Humanitarian Feedback Mechanisms: Research, Evidence and Guidance
Organisation: ALNAP and CDA Collaborative Learning Projects (Bonino, Jean and Knox Clarke)
Why this source: Evidence on what makes feedback mechanisms work, judged by the communities using them, with three case studies. Helps you choose channels and avoid token suggestion boxes.
What to look for: The findings on features of effective mechanisms and the case studies from Sudan, Pakistan and Haiti.
Use in lesson: Use it when you choose channels for different groups and plan how to close the loop with people.

Module: Module 06 · MEAL: Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability & Learning
Learning objective: Plan a learning routine with regular reviews, simple formats and recorded decisions, and know how to adapt plans openly when evidence says so.
Recommended source: Making Adaptive Rigour Work: Principles and Practices for Strengthening MEL for Adaptive Management
Organisation: Overseas Development Institute (ODI), GLAM (Leni Wild and Anne Buffardi)
Why this source: Shows how to keep adaptation rigorous, so changes follow good evidence rather than hunches. Ties learning routines to data quality, resourcing and incentives.
What to look for: The three principles and the inventory of practices in the briefing paper.
Use in lesson: Use it when you plan review meetings and agree who decides what to change.

Module: Module 06 · MEAL: Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability & Learning
Learning objective: Plan a learning routine with regular reviews, simple formats and recorded decisions, and know how to adapt plans openly when evidence says so.
Why this source: A simple method for a structured, honest team debrief, matching the lesson's format of what was planned, what happened, why and what we will change.
What to look for: The method description and the linked examples and resources on the page.
Use in lesson: Use it to run your first after-action review and record decisions with an owner and a date.

Module: Module 06 · MEAL: Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability & Learning
Learning objective: Plan a learning routine with regular reviews, simple formats and recorded decisions, and know how to adapt plans openly when evidence says so.
Recommended source: Adaptive Management: What It Means for Civil Society Organisations
Why this source: Written for NGOs, it explains what adaptive management needs from culture, funding and partners, and how to discuss changing plans with funders. UK network, global relevance.
What to look for: The sections on adaptive programmes, funding adaptation and partnership, and the practical tips for programme teams and leaders.
Use in lesson: Use it when you plan how to change activities, targets or your Theory of Change openly and agree changes with funders.

Module: Module 06 · MEAL: Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability & Learning
Learning objective: Build a reporting plan by audience that reports honestly, separating outputs from outcomes and contribution from attribution.
Why this source: Five principles and a checklist for judging whether evidence is good enough to report, including contribution and transparency. Created by a UK NGO network, but written for NGOs worldwide.
What to look for: The principles and the checklist; read the contribution and transparency principles before you write up results.
Use in lesson: Use the checklist to review a draft report before it goes to the board or funders, and to state its limits honestly.

Module: Module 06 · MEAL: Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability & Learning
Learning objective: Build a reporting plan by audience that reports honestly, separating outputs from outcomes and contribution from attribution.
Recommended source: Report and Support Use of Findings (Rainbow Framework)
Why this source: Helps you plan reports around what each user needs and how they will use findings, matching the audience-by-audience reporting plan.
What to look for: The page's guidance on developing findings in useful formats for the intended users and supporting them to act on the findings.
Use in lesson: Use it when you build your reporting plan by audience and decide how to share findings with communities.

Learning objective: Tell brand, identity, image, marketing and communications apart, and say how each applies to your organisation.
Why this source: 0 added. This is a short concept lesson and most free sources only repeat definitions. The one nonprofit-specific framework (Brand IDEA, Kylander and Stone) lives in 7.strategy, where it supports the brand platform, and it also explains the identity-versus-image gap taught here.

Learning objective: Turn positioning into a brand platform: purpose, promise, audiences, personality, key messages and proof points.
Recommended source: The Role of Brand in the Nonprofit Sector (Brand IDEA)
Organisation: Stanford Social Innovation Review (Nathalie Kylander and Christopher Stone)
Why this source: Research-based nonprofit brand framework (integrity, democracy, ethics, affinity). It shows why a promise must match what you actually deliver, which a business-brand guide would not.
What to look for: The four Brand IDEA principles, especially integrity (identity, image and mission aligned) and democracy (trusting staff and partners to carry the brand).
Use in lesson: Use it when writing your brand platform, to test that the promise, personality and proof points match your mission and real practice.

Learning objective: Define three or four personality traits, a voice with this-not-that pairs, and a word list that respects the people you serve.
Recommended source: Mailchimp Content Style Guide: Voice and Tone
Why this source: A short, openly licensed example of separating voice (constant) from tone (changes with the reader's mood). Written by a company, but a clear model to copy.
What to look for: 'Voice' versus 'Tone' and the guidance on adjusting tone to the reader's emotional state. Licence is CC BY-NC 4.0, so non-commercial reuse with credit is fine.
Use in lesson: Use it when drafting your this-not-that pairs and when you rewrite a real email or post to test your voice.

Learning objective: Define three or four personality traits, a voice with this-not-that pairs, and a word list that respects the people you serve.
Why this source: Gives tested wording alternatives for development and humanitarian communications, such as 'people we work with' instead of 'beneficiaries', with the reasons. Directly supports a dignified word list.
What to look for: Chapter 1 'The Power of Language', then 'Race, Power and Decolonization' and the sections relevant to your participants. Treat suggestions as context-dependent and ask communities.
Use in lesson: Use it when building your 'words we use and avoid' list and the line describing the people you serve.

Learning objective: Define three or four personality traits, a voice with this-not-that pairs, and a word list that respects the people you serve.
Recommended source: A Storyteller's Guide to Reframing Africa
Organisation: Africa No Filter (Lerato Mogoatlhe; editor Liz Sparg)
Why this source: An Africa-led guide to how stereotypes shape language and imagery, with a nine-question self-check. Adds a Global South view of what 'helpless' framing does.
What to look for: 'The Danger of a Single Story', 'Take Back the Pen' and 'Be Your Own Watchdog' with its checklist. PDF is hosted by Development Education Ireland.
Use in lesson: Use it when testing your voice and word list against a real draft, whatever region you work in.

Learning objective: Map how your organisation, programmes and trading arms relate, choose a naming model and check a name is safe to use.
Recommended source: Making a Mark: An Introduction to Trademarks for Small and Medium-sized Enterprises
Why this source: Plain international guide to choosing, searching and protecting a name or logo. Covers what the lesson says only briefly: trademark conflicts and domain names. Written for SMEs, so useful for social enterprises and hybrids.
What to look for: Chapters 'Creating Trademarks', 'Protecting Trademarks' and 'Using Trademarks' (domain names). Skim 'Trademarks Abroad' if you work across borders.
Use in lesson: Use it when you shortlist names and run the availability and infringement checks before you register or print anything.

Learning objective: Define a simple, consistent and accessible visual identity: logo, colour, typography, imagery and layout rules.
Organisation: World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) Web Accessibility Initiative
Why this source: Gives the exact contrast thresholds behind 'check colour contrast' (4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text) and explains why. Turns a vague rule into something you can test.
What to look for: The 'Intent' and 'Description' sections, and the large-text definition. Note the exemption for logos, so palettes still need testing for text use.
Use in lesson: Use it when you choose your two or three main colours and decide which pairs are allowed for text.

Learning objective: Define a simple, consistent and accessible visual identity: logo, colour, typography, imagery and layout rules.
Why this source: A free tool where you paste two hex codes and see whether they pass WCAG AA and AAA. Quicker and more reliable than judging by eye.
What to look for: Enter foreground and background hex codes, then read the pass/fail for normal text, large text and graphics.
Use in lesson: Use it to test every text-and-background pair in your palette and record the passing pairs in your guidelines.

Learning objective: Outline short, usable brand guidelines with templates and clear rules for co-branding with partners and funders.
Recommended source: Communicating and raising EU visibility: Guidance for external actions
Why this source: A real funder rulebook for logo use, acknowledgement wording and approvals. It shows what co-branding rules look like from the funder's side, so you can write yours to fit.
What to look for: The emblem and 'Funded by the European Union' statement rules, the no-separate-logo rule, and approval steps. The linked FAQ explains common edge cases.
Use in lesson: Use it when drafting your co-branding rules: whose logo leads, required acknowledgements and when partners or funders must approve.

Learning objective: Audit the trust signals your audiences look for and plan how to close the most important gaps.
Recommended source: Research into public trust in charities and trustees' experience of their role 2024
Organisation: Charity Commission for England and Wales
Why this source: Evidence on what the public looks for before trusting a charity: money well used, visible impact, ethical conduct and available financial information. UK public only, but the signals travel.
What to look for: The sections on drivers of trust, financial transparency and the reassurance of registration status. Remember the sample is the UK public.
Use in lesson: Use it when ranking which trust signals matter most to your supporters and funders in the audit.

Learning objective: Audit the trust signals your audiences look for and plan how to close the most important gaps.
Organisation: Accountable Now and eight partner accountability networks
Why this source: Developed through consultation with over 1,500 civil society organisations worldwide. Its 12 commitments define what an accountable organisation should show: transparency, feedback and responsiveness, governance and resource management.
What to look for: The 12 Commitments handbook and the Rendir self-assessment app. Use the commitments as a checklist for what to publish and prove.
Use in lesson: Use it when you list your trust signals and decide which published policies, reports or feedback routes to add first.

Learning objective: Set up light brand governance: an owner, approval levels, an asset library and an annual review.
Why this source: 0 added. No open, authoritative source on nonprofit brand governance was found that goes beyond the lesson; most results are agency or software blogs. The 'brand democracy' principle in Brand IDEA (see 7.strategy) supports the light-touch approach taught here.

Learning objective: Write two to four measurable communication objectives, each linked to a strategic objective.
Why this source: A free six-step planning tool built for nonprofits and foundations. It forces the order the lesson teaches: objectives first, then audiences, messages and tactics, with evaluation built in.
What to look for: Work through the six steps in order and save your chart. Concentrate on the objectives and audiences steps for this lesson.
Use in lesson: Use it to draft your communication objectives and check each one links to a strategic objective and a measure.

Learning objective: Define priority audience segments by need and write one evidence-based persona.
Why this source: Short, research-based explanation of what a persona is and is not. Stresses that personas must come from real research, and warns against irrelevant detail and stereotypes.
What to look for: How to build personas from interviews, surveys and field data, the list of useful components, and the caveats section.
Use in lesson: Use it when you write your persona, to keep it evidence-based and focused on goals, barriers and trusted channels.

Learning objective: Define priority audience segments by need and write one evidence-based persona.
Why this source: Shows how to involve disabled people, ethnic minorities and community groups from the start rather than consulting at the end. Helps you ground personas in lived experience.
What to look for: The steps on early engagement, testing with different groups and shared decision-making. Written for UK government, so adapt the examples.
Use in lesson: Use it when you test your persona and segments with real members of each audience, especially communities you serve.

Learning objective: Write a core message, supporting messages, proof points and one audience version, and test them.
Why this source: A well-used one-page structure for separating your core message from the points that support it and what each audience gains. Made for scientists, but works for any expert explaining complex work.
What to look for: The Message Box layout and the worked examples in the workbook. Ignore science-specific wording.
Use in lesson: Use it to draft your core message and supporting messages, then adapt the box for each audience version.

Learning objective: Write a core message, supporting messages, proof points and one audience version, and test them.
Why this source: Explains why facts alone rarely persuade and how context, messengers, numbers and tone change what people hear. Dated (2005) and US-based, but the core principles hold.
What to look for: Section III on elements of the frame (context, numbers, messengers, tone) and the framing checklist in Section IV.
Use in lesson: Use it when choosing proof points and testing whether your message explains the problem as well as the solution.

Learning objective: Write ethical storytelling rules covering consent, dignity, risk and a consent log.
Recommended source: Putting the People in the Pictures First: Ethical guidelines for the production and use of content (2024 update)
Why this source: Written for NGOs. Covers consent as ongoing dialogue, responsible portrayal, power and racism in NGO imagery, emergencies and AI images, with a one-page Statement of Ethical Practice.
What to look for: The informed consent chapter, responsible portrayal, the child-protection safeguards (including renewing consent after three years) and the practical checklist items on storing consent evidence separately.
Use in lesson: Use it when writing your storytelling rules and designing your consent log fields, expiry dates and withdrawal process.

Learning objective: Write ethical storytelling rules covering consent, dignity, risk and a consent log.
Why this source: Short principles and interview rules for children. A specific reference for the 'extra care with children' paragraph. Aimed at journalists, so adapt for your own staff.
What to look for: The principles and interview guidelines, especially anonymising and protecting children and avoiding stereotypes.
Use in lesson: Use it before you collect or publish any story or image involving a child, and copy the relevant rules into yours.

Learning objective: Plan a website structure around audience tasks and a set of practical discoverability actions.
Recommended source: Easy Checks: A first review of web accessibility
Why this source: A quick, non-technical way to test your own pages for accessibility problems. Turns the long standard into ten checks anyone can run in a browser.
What to look for: Checks on page titles, image alt text, headings, colour contrast, text resizing, keyboard use and forms. Passing them does not prove full accessibility.
Use in lesson: Use it each time you review the site, and when you commission or check a web designer's work.

Learning objective: Plan a website structure around audience tasks and a set of practical discoverability actions.
Why this source: The international standard for accessible web content. Useful as the reference your brief to a developer should cite (Level AA).
What to look for: The four principles (perceivable, operable, understandable, robust) and the Level AA success criteria. Use the linked 'Quick Reference' rather than reading end to end.
Use in lesson: Use it when writing a website brief or checking compliance claims, for example 'meets WCAG 2.2 AA'.

Learning objective: Plan a website structure around audience tasks and a set of practical discoverability actions.
Why this source: The search engine's own plain guidance on what helps pages be found: clear titles and descriptions, useful content and honest practice. Includes a section on common myths.
What to look for: The sections on getting found, site organisation, content quality and how pages appear in results (titles and descriptions), plus the common-misconceptions section. Updated December 2025.
Use in lesson: Use it when you set page titles and descriptions and decide your discoverability actions, without paying for tricks.

Learning objective: Choose one or two social channels and define each channel's purpose, content mix and safety rules.
Organisation: DataReportal (Kepios, We Are Social and Meltwater)
Why this source: Free, country-by-country data on internet and social media use, helping you choose channels from evidence rather than habit. Covers regions where WhatsApp or Facebook dominate.
What to look for: Social media use by platform, and the country reports linked from the page. Check your own country and your audience's age and gender.
Use in lesson: Use it when checking whether your priority audience actually uses the channels you are considering.

Learning objective: Choose one or two social channels and define each channel's purpose, content mix and safety rules.
Recommended source: Using Social Media in Community Based Protection: A Guide
Why this source: Shows how to use social media with vulnerable communities while managing privacy, safety and inequality risks. A strong source for the safety rules the lesson asks you to set.
What to look for: The guide's risk and protocol sections, plus the free five-hour e-course. Written for refugee protection, so adapt to your context.
Use in lesson: Use it when writing who can post, moderation and data protection rules, and when deciding if a private response channel is safer.

Learning objective: Build a consent-based email list, a newsletter and one welcome journey, and know which rules apply.
Recommended source: Guidance on direct marketing using electronic mail
Why this source: Official UK rules for email marketing, including the new charitable-purposes soft opt-in (in force 5 Feb 2026). Shows what 'clear consent' means in practice. UK law only.
What to look for: The sections on consent, the soft opt-in for charities and the opt-out requirements. The soft opt-in applies only to contact details collected on or after 5 February 2026.
Use in lesson: Use it when you design your sign-up form, consent wording and unsubscribe process, if you email UK recipients.

Learning objective: Build a consent-based email list, a newsletter and one welcome journey, and know which rules apply.
Recommended source: CAN-SPAM Act: A Compliance Guide for Business
Why this source: A short plain-English guide to seven rules for commercial email in the US: honest headers and subjects, a postal address and a working opt-out. Useful if you email US recipients.
What to look for: The seven requirements, and the notes that opt-outs must be honoured within 10 business days. US law only.
Use in lesson: Use it as a checklist for your email footer and unsubscribe handling when your list includes US recipients.

Learning objective: Define content pillars and draft a month of an editorial calendar that fits your capacity.
Why this source: Shows how to turn audience insight into user-need statements before planning content. Prevents calendars built around what you want to say rather than what people need.
What to look for: The user-need statement format, the warning against 'solutionising', and the list of research methods (analytics, interviews, surveys, card sorting).
Use in lesson: Use it before you fill in the audience and message columns of your calendar, to set your content pillars.

Learning objective: Write a campaign brief with goal, audience, call to action and risks, and know the legal limits on advocacy.
Why this source: A five-step campaign planning model (objectives, audience insight, strategy, implementation, scoring) that matches the brief. The PDF is a four-to-five-page practical guide. Written for government, but widely used.
What to look for: Each of the five steps, and the split between outputs, outtakes and outcomes. Suggests spending 5 to 10% of paid-campaign budgets on evaluation.
Use in lesson: Use it as the skeleton of your campaign brief, especially the objective, audience and 'scoring' sections.

Learning objective: Write a campaign brief with goal, audience, call to action and risks, and know the legal limits on advocacy.
Recommended source: Campaigning and political activity guidance for charities (CC9)
Organisation: Charity Commission for England and Wales
Why this source: Official explanation of what registered charities may campaign on and the limit on political activity. A clear model of what 'legal limits' means. England and Wales only.
What to look for: The main guidance on campaigning in support of charitable purposes, and the separate section on elections and referendums.
Use in lesson: Use it when your campaign touches policy or elections, to check trustees' duties before you publish. Elsewhere, check your own regulator.

Learning objective: Write a campaign brief with goal, audience, call to action and risks, and know the legal limits on advocacy.
Why this source: Country-by-country summaries of laws affecting association, expression and assembly. A global starting point for the legal and safety risks of advocacy outside the UK.
What to look for: Find your country, then read the sections on freedom of association and expression. Use them to flag risks to partners and participants.
Use in lesson: Use it when you complete the 'risks and approvals' part of your brief for advocacy or awareness campaigns.

Learning objective: Design one community you will build, with ways for people to take part, moderation rules and engagement measures.
Recommended source: Minimum Quality Standards and Indicators in Community Engagement
Why this source: Sixteen minimum standards on six principles, developed with NGOs, governments and academics. Moves from broadcasting to participation and gives indicators to track it.
What to look for: The summary version first (short), then the standards on participation, inclusion and two-way communication. Available in four languages.
Use in lesson: Use it when you decide how people will take part, hold roles and give feedback, and what 'participation' measures to track.

Learning objective: Design one community you will build, with ways for people to take part, moderation rules and engagement measures.
Organisation: IFRC (International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies)
Why this source: Practical tools used by Red Cross and Red Crescent societies, which are rooted in local volunteers. Covers listening, feedback and community participation.
What to look for: The CEA Guide and the minimum actions for community engagement and accountability in programmes. Pick the tools that match your size.
Use in lesson: Use it when planning your events, feedback routes and moderation, and when choosing ways to listen more than you broadcast.

Learning objective: Prepare a press kit checklist and a short media list, and agree rules for protecting participants.
Why this source: A civil society toolkit on how newsrooms work, giving interviews and writing press statements, including when media attention is hostile. Global, civil-society-focused. Dated (2011), so check platforms.
What to look for: How newsrooms work, interview advice for print, radio and TV, and the press statement section.
Use in lesson: Use it when you prepare key messages, choose who can speak to the media and draft your press kit.

Learning objective: Prepare a press kit checklist and a short media list, and agree rules for protecting participants.
Recommended source: Interviewing resources (Ethics and Practice: Interviewing Victims; Essential Tips for Interviewing Children)
Organisation: Global Center for Journalism and Trauma (formerly the Dart Center)
Why this source: Shows what a trauma-aware interview looks like, from the journalist's side. Helps you prepare participants, set boundaries and judge when an interview should not go ahead.
What to look for: 'Ethics and Practice: Interviewing Victims', 'Essential Tips for Interviewing Children' and the sexual and gender-based violence interview guide. Creative Commons licensed.
Use in lesson: Use it when you brief participants and decide your support and consent steps before any media interview.

Lesson: 8.12 Reputation, crisis communication and social media policy
Learning objective: Draft crisis communication essentials and social media rules, and know who must be informed.
Why this source: A structured crisis plan on four pillars: strategy, tactics, organisation, people. Covers holding lines, contact lists, clearance and what to do in the first hour, day and week.
What to look for: The holding lines, contact list and clearance sections, and the first hour, day and week timeline. Written for government, so scale it down.
Use in lesson: Use it as the checklist for your crisis essentials: who leads, holding statements and who must be informed.

Lesson: 8.12 Reputation, crisis communication and social media policy
Learning objective: Draft crisis communication essentials and social media rules, and know who must be informed.
Recommended source: How to report a serious incident in your charity
Organisation: Charity Commission for England and Wales
Why this source: Official list of incidents trustees must report (safeguarding, fraud, data breaches, reputational harm) and who else to notify, such as police, ICO and local authority. UK only; use it as a model elsewhere.
What to look for: 'What to report' and 'who to tell', including the point that trustees are responsible for reporting as soon as reasonably possible.
Use in lesson: Use it when you list your likely scenarios and the regulators, funders and partners you must inform.

Lesson: 8.12 Reputation, crisis communication and social media policy
Learning objective: Draft crisis communication essentials and social media rules, and know who must be informed.
Organisation: Charity Commission for England and Wales
Why this source: Explains trustees' duties and risks when charities use social media, and includes a policy checklist you can adapt. England and Wales only, but the checklist is useful anywhere.
What to look for: The main guidance on risk and trustee responsibility, and the policy checklist (ODT file) for building or reviewing a social media policy.
Use in lesson: Use it when you draft your social media rules for official accounts, staff and volunteers, and escalation.

Learning objective: Define outcome measures for each communication objective and set a regular review routine.
Organisation: AMEC (International Association for the Measurement and Evaluation of Communication)
Why this source: The professional body's free, non-proprietary framework. Separates outputs, out-takes and outcomes, links measures to objectives and is translated into 25 languages.
What to look for: The interactive framework tiles and the taxonomy of measures. Start with objectives, then choose outcome measures.
Use in lesson: Use it to pick one or two outcome measures per communication objective and fill the gaps in your review routine.

Learning objective: Define outcome measures for each communication objective and set a regular review routine.
Recommended source: Evaluate and learn: evaluating low- and no-cost communications
Why this source: Built for communications that have no big budget. A decision tree helps you choose Basic, Enhanced or Comprehensive evaluation and track qualitative and quantitative signals.
What to look for: 'Choosing your evaluation tier' and the decision tree, plus the six stages from inputs to learning. Some templates may need membership.
Use in lesson: Use it when you set your measures for each objective and decide how much effort each deserves.

Lesson: 9.1 Finance roles and the finance cycle
Learning objective: Decide who does what in your finance function and set out your monthly and annual finance cycle.
Organisation: Charity Commission for England and Wales
Why this source: A plain statement of what a governing body must oversee, so the split between founder, bookkeeper and board rests on real duties rather than guesswork.
What to look for: Read the five headings: protect the money, know your position, keep records, manage expenses, and deal with problems early.
Use in lesson: Use it when writing your roles and monthly cycle. Adapt the duties to your own legal form and country.

Learning objective: Draft an organisational budget from your annual plan, with clear headings and written assumptions.
Recommended source: Defining budgets and cashflow forecasts and writing a budget
Why this source: Treats a budget as a loop from action plan to costs and income to feasibility, and insists you record assumptions, which our lesson asks for.
What to look for: The 'Writing a budget' section: the flowchart, and the advice to build on an action plan and document every assumption.
Use in lesson: Use it to draft your budget headings and assumptions, and to test whether the plan is affordable before the board approves it.

Lesson: 9.3 Project budgets, cost allocation and full cost recovery
Learning objective: Build a project budget that includes a fair, consistently allocated share of support costs.
Earlier sources (action): Costing and Financing of Small-scale WASH Projects [REMOVE]
Why this source: Explains direct costs versus shared costs and how to share the latter fairly, with a worked example.
What to look for: The worked example, where a £7,500 direct cost rises to £8,500 once support costs are shared, and the allocation bases: people, floor space, expenditure.
Use in lesson: Use it to choose allocation bases and calculate the support-cost share in your exercise budget.

Lesson: 9.3 Project budgets, cost allocation and full cost recovery
Learning objective: Build a project budget that includes a fair, consistently allocated share of support costs.
Earlier sources (action): Costing and Financing of Small-scale WASH Projects [REMOVE]
Recommended source: Administration Costs Research: The Overhead Myth
Organisation: Humentum (for Funders for Real Cost, Real Change)
Why this source: Evidence from 81 national NGOs that funders routinely under-cover administration costs. It gives you data, from outside the global North, to back your indirect cost rate.
What to look for: The executive summary (also in Spanish and Portuguese): how project grants fall short of a full share of administration costs.
Use in lesson: Use it when you work out your real indirect cost rate and prepare to negotiate it with funders.

Lesson: 9.3 Project budgets, cost allocation and full cost recovery
Learning objective: Build a project budget that includes a fair, consistently allocated share of support costs.

Learning objective: Set up a funds register that shows which money is restricted, designated or free to use, and keep it separate in the books.

Learning objective: Draft a twelve-month cash flow forecast and set the runway level that triggers action.

Use in lesson: Use it to build your forecast, then set your runway trigger from the pessimistic version.

Learning objective: Map one money flow with its checks, and write procurement thresholds that fit your size and funders.
Organisation: Charity Commission for England and Wales
Why this source: The clearest free statement of separation of duties, reconciliations and compensating controls, with an internal financial controls checklist you can adapt.
What to look for: 'General principles for all charities', the sections on banking, income and expenditure, and the checklist near the end.
Use in lesson: Use it to design the checks on the money flow you map. Adapt to your local law.

Learning objective: Map one money flow with its checks, and write procurement thresholds that fit your size and funders.
Why this source: Shows how to turn controls into a written manual: delegated authority, segregation of duties, conflicts, income and expenditure procedures and record keeping.
What to look for: 'Financial responsibilities' and the expenditure and income sections. Note that some sub-pages and templates need NCVO login.
Use in lesson: Use it to structure your written approval limits and checks once you have mapped the money flow.

Learning objective: Map one money flow with its checks, and write procurement thresholds that fit your size and funders.
Why this source: Free procurement request form and comparative bid analysis built for NGOs, turning thresholds into a working approval step.
What to look for: The two templates: the procurement form, and the comparative bid analysis for scoring supplier quotes side by side.
Use in lesson: Use them to put your thresholds into practice: when quotes are needed, who approves, and the reason a supplier was chosen.

Lesson: 9.7 Management accounts and budget versus actual
Learning objective: Design a short monthly or quarterly report that compares budget with actual, explains variances and forecasts the year end.
Recommended source: Academy trust management accounting: good practice guide
Why this source: A government guide that sets out a simple management pack: income and expenditure, variation to budget and rolling cash flow, with explicit permission to adapt it to your audience.
What to look for: The recommended sections and the advice on tailoring the pack for different readers. Ignore school-specific lines.
Use in lesson: Use it as a layout for your report: variance explanation, forecast to year end and cash outlook.

Lesson: 9.8 Financial reporting: board, funders and statutory
Learning objective: Build a financial reporting calendar covering board, funder, statutory and investor reports, each with an owner and data source.
Why this source: A shared narrative template agreed by donors and agencies to cut duplicate reporting. It is useful evidence when you ask funders to accept one report format.
