Use in lesson: Use it when building your calendar: ask each funder whether it accepts a common format, and reconcile figures to your accounts.

Learning objective: Write down which external scrutiny applies to you, how the board oversees money, and your reserves policy.
Organisation: Charity Commission for England and Wales
Why this source: Explains how to justify a reserves level from your own risks and income stability rather than a fixed rule, and how to explain it publicly.
What to look for: 'Key messages for trustees' and Annex 1, the three-question approach for smaller charities.
Use in lesson: Use it to write your reserves policy: the target, the reason for it, and what happens when you are above or below it.

Learning objective: Write down which external scrutiny applies to you, how the board oversees money, and your reserves policy.
Recommended source: Changes to charity accounting and reporting
Organisation: Charity Commission for England and Wales
Why this source: Shows, for one jurisdiction, how thresholds for independent examination and audit and the accounting standard change. A reminder to check each year what applies to you.
What to look for: The new income thresholds for examination and audit from 30 September 2026, and the SORP 2026 changes for periods starting 1 January 2026.
Use in lesson: Use it as a model for questions to ask your accountant: thresholds, deadlines, who may examine, and what funders require.

Learning objective: Choose a small set of financial health measures and record their current values.
Why this source: A free self-assessment for small and medium NGOs across planning, accounting, controls, staffing, grants management and reporting. It scores financial health and points to weak spots.
What to look for: The six areas it scores, and which weaknesses it says need a professional rather than a quick fix.
Use in lesson: Use it once your measures are chosen, to test the wider finance system behind the numbers.

Learning objective: Choose a small set of financial health measures and record their current values.
Recommended source: Best Practices for Nonprofit Financial Health, Part One: Top 3 Measures
Why this source: Defines three simple measures, consistent surpluses, positive unrestricted net worth and liquidity, and shows how to calculate months of cash and months of available net assets.
What to look for: The months of cash and available net assets ratios, and the advice for smaller organisations to work towards targets in steps.
Use in lesson: Use it to calculate your reserve measure. Treat its six-month liquidity benchmark as a US reference point, not a rule.

Learning objective: Build a legal and regulatory map showing each obligation, regulator, deadline and owner, and what a local adviser has confirmed.
Earlier sources (action): The Essential Trustee: What You Need to Know (CC3) [MOVE]
Why this source: Country reports on the laws shaping how civil society organisations register, operate and receive funding. Helpful when you work outside the UK and need local questions to ask.
What to look for: Open the report for each country you work in and note the rules on registration, funding and reporting.
Use in lesson: Use it to fill the regulator and obligation columns for each country, then confirm gaps with a qualified local adviser.

Lesson: 10.2 Working out which policies you actually need
Learning objective: Work out which policies you need now, soon and as good practice, with an owner and approval route for each.
Why this source: Separates a minimum set of essential policies from those needed as you grow (around 30 staff), which matches our sorting into required now, required soon and good practice.
What to look for: 'Essential policies and procedures' and 'Others to consider', plus the advice to involve staff in writing them.
Use in lesson: Use it to sort your draft register into three groups. Then adjust for your country, activities and funders.

Learning objective: Set up a contracts register and a pre-signature checklist so you know obligations, dates and who may sign.
Recommended source: TrustLaw: free legal support for NGOs and social enterprises
Why this source: Connects eligible NGOs and social enterprises with law firms that give free advice on transactional matters such as contracts, for when a significant or unusual agreement needs legal review.
What to look for: The eligibility rules: legally incorporated, at least a year of operation, transactional advice only (no litigation), plus the free orientation call.
Use in lesson: Use it when a contract on your register is high-value or unusual, before anyone signs.

Lesson: 10.4 Core policies: conduct, conflicts and anti-fraud
Learning objective: Outline your core conduct, conflict of interest, anti-fraud and anti-harassment policies and how each will be put into practice.
Recommended source: Identifying and managing conflicts of interest in a charity (CC29)
Organisation: Charity Commission for England and Wales
Why this source: A step-by-step process for spotting, declaring and managing conflicts, rooted in the duty to act in the organisation's best interests.
What to look for: The definition of a conflict and the step-by-step process for managing one.
Use in lesson: Use it to draft your conflict of interest policy, including how declarations are recorded and reviewed.

Lesson: 10.4 Core policies: conduct, conflicts and anti-fraud
Learning objective: Outline your core conduct, conflict of interest, anti-fraud and anti-harassment policies and how each will be put into practice.
Recommended source: Handbook of good practices: Preventing corruption in humanitarian operations
Why this source: Shows where corruption enters aid delivery and which controls help. Useful when deciding what your anti-fraud and bribery policy must prohibit and monitor.
What to look for: Pick the parts that match your activities, such as procurement, staffing or distributions. Available in English, French, Spanish and Arabic.
Use in lesson: Use it to test whether your outline covers the real fraud and bribery risks of your programmes.

Learning objective: Outline a proportionate safeguarding framework, without case details, with local reporting pathways.
Organisation: Safeguarding Resource and Support Hub (funded by UK FCDO and Swiss SDC)
Why this source: A free library of more than 1,300 policy guides, templates, training materials and pocket guides, built for civil society organisations in the aid sector.
What to look for: Start with the policy guidance, code of conduct templates and how-to notes. Filter by language and country.
Use in lesson: Use it to check each element of your framework outline: policy, safer recruitment, reporting routes, response and survivor support.

Learning objective: Outline a proportionate safeguarding framework, without case details, with local reporting pathways.
Why this source: A step-by-step guide to putting protection from sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment into practice, with case studies from other organisations.
What to look for: The chapter on each implementation step, and the case studies of how other organisations did it.
Use in lesson: Use it to turn your framework outline into an ordered plan of actions with owners.

Learning objective: Outline a proportionate safeguarding framework, without case details, with local reporting pathways.
Why this source: Four standards (policy, people, procedures, accountability) tied to the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, for any organisation whose work touches children.
What to look for: The four standards and their requirements, for a quick check of your outline.
Use in lesson: Use it if you work with or near children, to test your framework against an international benchmark.

Learning objective: Build a data inventory and list the privacy actions you need, checked against the law where you work.
Recommended source: Getting started with data protection: a step-by-step guide
Why this source: A practical eight-step sequence for small organisations: list personal data, find a lawful reason, secure it, explain it, handle requests and report breaches.
What to look for: The steps on cataloguing personal data, privacy notices and breach reporting (72 hours under UK rules).
Use in lesson: Use it as the working order for your data inventory and privacy action list. UK law only; check your own country.

Learning objective: Build a data inventory and list the privacy actions you need, checked against the law where you work.
Recommended source: Data Protection and Privacy Legislation Worldwide
Why this source: A global tracker showing which countries have data protection laws, so you can see whether your own country has one and start the conversation with a local adviser.
What to look for: Look up each country you work in and note whether a law exists. Follow the link to the legislation.
Use in lesson: Use it to add a 'law that applies' column to your inventory for each country.

Learning objective: Build a data inventory and list the privacy actions you need, checked against the law where you work.
Recommended source: Handbook on Data Protection in Humanitarian Action (3rd edition)
Organisation: International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC)
Why this source: Applies data protection principles to work with vulnerable people in fragile settings, including new risks from digital identity, social media and AI.
What to look for: The chapters on the legal basis for processing and on sharing data with partners, for programmes that hold sensitive data.
Use in lesson: Use it when your inventory includes health, ethnicity or data about children, or sharing with partners.

Learning objective: Design clear reporting channels and timescales for concerns, complaints and incidents, including duties to regulators and funders.
Why this source: A practical guide and policy framework for building a whistleblowing policy and a culture where people feel safe to speak up. Free in English, French and Arabic.
What to look for: The policy framework, and the advice for leaders on why to invest in protection from retaliation.
Use in lesson: Use it to draft your whistleblowing route, including reporting outside the line of management.

Learning objective: Design clear reporting channels and timescales for concerns, complaints and incidents, including duties to regulators and funders.
Why this source: A best-practice guide, ready templates and e-learning for setting up complaints and feedback mechanisms that work for people your organisation serves, whatever its size.
What to look for: The toolkit templates and examples, and the best-practice guide on how complaints are received, handled and learned from.
Use in lesson: Use it to set timescales, independent review and learning from patterns for your complaints channel.

Learning objective: Design clear reporting channels and timescales for concerns, complaints and incidents, including duties to regulators and funders.
Recommended source: How to report a serious incident in your charity
Organisation: Charity Commission for England and Wales
Why this source: A worked example of external reporting duties: what counts as serious, who must report, and that reports must be prompt, as soon as reasonably possible.
What to look for: The categories of reportable incident and the 'promptly' requirement. Note the annual return declaration for charities over £25,000.
Use in lesson: Use it as a model when listing which incidents must go to regulators, funders or insurers, and by when, in your own context.

Learning objective: List the HR and workplace policies you need, their legal status for your country, and owners and review dates.
Recommended source: NATLEX: Database of national labour, social security and related human rights legislation
Why this source: The ILO's free database of national labour laws. It lets you see what employment law says in your country before you write or copy a policy.
What to look for: Search by country and subject (working time, discrimination, occupational safety, dismissal). Available in English, French and Spanish.
Use in lesson: Use it to check each policy against the law of the country where the person works, then confirm with a local adviser.

Learning objective: List the HR and workplace policies you need, their legal status for your country, and owners and review dates.
Why this source: Free sample policies for small organisations: disciplinary, grievance, flexible working, expenses, dignity at work, equity and inclusion and leave. Use as a starting point only.
What to look for: The disciplinary, grievance and dignity at work samples. Check pages 2 and 3 for more.
Use in lesson: Use them to see what a short, usable policy looks like; then rewrite for your country's law.

Learning objective: List the HR and workplace policies you need, their legal status for your country, and owners and review dates.
Why this source: Sets out what a volunteer policy covers: recruitment, induction, expenses, supervision, health and safety, confidentiality and complaints, with advice to review it yearly.
What to look for: The list of what the policy should cover and the advice to tailor it to your size.
Use in lesson: Use it to build the lighter volunteer framework your list needs.

Learning objective: Draft one priority procedure with trigger, role, steps, records and exceptions, and plan a walkthrough with someone who did not write it.
Why this source: Free model documents showing how a rule becomes steps, in particular a complaints-handling policy paired with its procedure, plus conflict of interest and dispute-resolution templates.
What to look for: The complaints-handling model policy and procedure, and the internal dispute resolution templates.
Use in lesson: Use them to see how a policy pairs with a procedure, then draft your own. Australian law, so adapt to yours.

Learning objective: Draft one priority procedure with trigger, role, steps, records and exceptions, and plan a walkthrough with someone who did not write it.

What to look for: 'Writing for understanding' and 'Test for understanding'.
Use in lesson: Use them to rewrite your draft procedure and plan the test with someone who did not write it.

Learning objective: Set up a policy register and review schedule covering owner, approval, acknowledgement and next review date.
Why this source: 0 resources. This lesson is about using the platform's policy register and onboarding tools, and the lifecycle is straightforward. The sources found cover which policies to write, not how to run review cycles, and a list would only repeat the lesson. NCVO's volunteer-policy page (10.8) does recommend yearly review.

Learning objective: Identify and assess your main risks as cause, event and consequence, scored for likelihood and impact before and after controls.
Organisation: Charity Commission for England and Wales
Why this source: A clear five-stage risk cycle with example registers showing gross and net risk, plus a catalogue of the risk areas charities commonly face.
What to look for: The risk management model, Annex 1 (register example) and Annex 2 (common risk areas: governance, operational, financial, external, compliance).
Use in lesson: Use Annex 2 as a prompt list when identifying risks, and Annex 1 for the register layout.

Learning objective: Identify and assess your main risks as cause, event and consequence, scored for likelihood and impact before and after controls.
Recommended source: Security Risk Management: a basic guide for smaller NGOs
Organisation: European Interagency Security Forum (EISF, now GISF)
Why this source: Written for small, resource-limited NGOs, with ready risk assessment matrices, travel risk forms and incident reporting frameworks that you can adapt.
What to look for: The risk assessment matrices and templates, and the chapters on fulfilling duty of care and incident monitoring.
Use in lesson: Use its matrices to score likelihood and impact, especially for risks to staff, travel and field work.

Learning objective: Identify and assess your main risks as cause, event and consequence, scored for likelihood and impact before and after controls.
Recommended source: The Orange Book: Management of Risk – Principles and Concepts
Why this source: A free, concise statement of risk management principles from a government that manages large public risks. Good for tightening how you define, score and compare risks.
What to look for: The principles of risk identification and assessment, and how controls reduce risk.
Use in lesson: Use it to sense-check your scoring approach and the difference between inherent and residual risk.

Lesson: 10.12 Risk registers, ownership, mitigation and escalation
Learning objective: Build a short risk register with one owner per risk, a chosen response, a stated risk appetite and clear escalation rules.
Recommended source: Risk appetite and tolerance: guidance for practitioners
Why this source: Separates risk appetite (willingness to take risk) from tolerance (capacity to bear it), with practical advice for organisations of any size. A free executive summary is available.
What to look for: The distinction between appetite and tolerance, and how to set measurable tolerance levels that can trigger escalation.
Use in lesson: Use it to set your appetite by area (low for safeguarding and legal, higher for innovation) and to write escalation thresholds.

Lesson: 10.12 Risk registers, ownership, mitigation and escalation
Learning objective: Build a short risk register with one owner per risk, a chosen response, a stated risk appetite and clear escalation rules.
Why this source: A free risk register framework for charities, on a page that also hosts a code of conduct and declaration of interests, handy for your 10.4 policies too.
What to look for: The risk register sample, found on page 1 of the sample documents list.
Use in lesson: Use it as a starting layout, then add columns for owner, response and escalation.

Lesson: 10.12 Risk registers, ownership, mitigation and escalation
Learning objective: Build a short risk register with one owner per risk, a chosen response, a stated risk appetite and clear escalation rules.
Recommended source: Security Risk-Sharing in Partnerships: Practical barriers and pathways for intermediaries
Why this source: Explains how risk is too often passed to local partners rather than shared, with case studies and nine pathways for fairer risk responses in partnerships.
What to look for: The seven barriers and the nine pathways, and the three organisational case studies.
Use in lesson: Use it when your 'transfer' response means passing risk to a partner, to check you are sharing it fairly and with the right support.

Learning objective: Set a review routine and early warning indicators so risks are checked regularly and linked to objectives.

Why this source: The original publisher's summary of a leading risk framework. It ties risk monitoring and review to strategy and performance, which supports linking risks to objectives and KPIs.
What to look for: 'Review and Revision', and 'Information, Communication and Reporting', on keeping risk information flowing up, down and across the organisation.
Use in lesson: Use it to justify linking each risk to objectives and review meetings. Treat the corporate wording as background only.

Module: Module 11 · Fundraising, Revenue & Sustainable Business Models

Module: Module 11 · Fundraising, Revenue & Sustainable Business Models

Module: Module 11 · Fundraising, Revenue & Sustainable Business Models
